title: Our Lady of Guadalupe (12 December)
hookLine: the patroness of the Americas; roses in December
last: FULL OF GRACE FROM THE START.

cards: Before dawn on December 12, in Mexico City and in parishes from Los Angeles to Chicago, people gather outside churches to sing Las Mañanitas, the birthday song, to Mary. Mariachis in the dark.
Roses everywhere, before a framed image of a young woman with her head bowed, dressed in a starred mantle, standing on a crescent moon. Her basilica in Mexico City stands at the foot of a hill.
The story behind all those roses begins with a poor man on that hill in winter.

teach.b: December 1531, in the years just after the Spanish conquest of the Aztec capital. Juan Diego, an Indigenous man and a recent convert, is walking past the hill of Tepeyac.
He hears birdsong, then a voice calling him by name. A young woman, speaking his own language, Nahuatl, tells him she is the Mother of the true God and asks for a church to be built there.

teach.h: THE BISHOP ASKS FOR A SIGN.
teach.b: He goes to the bishop, Juan de Zumárraga, who is unconvinced and asks for a sign.
Then Juan Diego's uncle falls gravely ill, and Juan Diego, embarrassed, takes a different path around the hill to fetch a priest and avoid her. She meets him anyway.
The best-known account gives her words, in paraphrase: do not be afraid; am I not here, I who am your mother?

She tells him his uncle is already healed and sends him up the hill, where in the cold of December he finds roses blooming. He gathers them into his tilma, his rough cloak, and carries them to the bishop.
When he opens it, the roses fall, and on the cloth is the image people still visit today.

The fullest account, the Nican Mopohua, was published in Nahuatl in 1649, and historians debate how early the story was written down; the Church's devotion rests on long tradition and on the image itself.
In 2002, Pope John Paul II canonized Juan Diego, and popes have named Mary under this title patroness of the Americas.
In the story, notice who she chooses: not the bishop, but a conquered man, addressed in his own tongue, by name.

how: On December 12 many Catholics, especially Mexican and Mexican-American communities, gather before dawn to sing Las Mañanitas to Our Lady of Guadalupe and bring roses to her image.

practice: Picture a church near you, its door, and the place by an image of Mary where people leave roses; if you can go today, you might bring one flower.

For now, think of someone who has said to you, in their own way, I'm here: a parent, a friend, a stranger in a hard hour. If you pray, offer that person to Our Lady; if not, simply give thanks for them.

wordCard.voice: Nican Mopohua, 'here it is told.' The Nahuatl account of Mary's appearance to Juan Diego at Tepeyac in 1531, published in 1649. Today's word.

orig.note: Nahuatl, written in Latin letters: 'here it is told', the opening words and title of the account.
